learningObjectives: melting point as a purity test

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a mixture?
options: Two or more substances chemically bonded together
A single type of atom only
Two or more substances not chemically bonded together
Atoms of two elements joined in a fixed ratio
questions.explain: In a mixture the substances are simply mixed and not chemically joined, so each keeps its own properties and they can be separated by physical means.

questions.q: In chemistry, a pure substance is best defined as one that:
options: Is safe to eat or drink
Consists of a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance
Has been filtered at least once
questions.explain: The scientific meaning of 'pure' is a single element or compound. This differs from everyday use (e.g. 'pure orange juice'), which is actually a mixture.

questions.q: A sample melts sharply at exactly one temperature. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: A pure substance melts (and boils) at a specific, sharp temperature. A mixture melts over a range of temperatures.

questions.q: Filtration is the best method to separate:
options: An insoluble solid from a liquid
questions.explain: Filtration separates an insoluble solid (residue on the filter paper) from the liquid (filtrate that passes through).

questions.q: To obtain pure salt crystals from salt solution, you would:
options: Evaporate the water so the salt crystallises
questions.explain: Evaporating (or gently heating then leaving to crystallise) removes the water and leaves solid salt crystals behind, because the salt is soluble.

questions.q: Why is slow crystallisation often preferred to rapid evaporation to dryness?
options: It needs no heat at all
questions.explain: Allowing the solution to cool and crystallise slowly gives larger, more regular crystals; boiling to dryness can decompose the solid and gives tiny crystals.

questions.q: Simple distillation is used to separate:
options: A soluble solid from its solvent, collecting the solvent
questions.explain: In simple distillation the solvent (e.g. water) evaporates, is cooled in the condenser and collected, leaving the dissolved solid behind. It works when boiling points differ greatly.

questions.q: In distillation, what is the job of the condenser?
options: To cool the vapour back into a liquid
questions.explain: Cold water flows through the outer jacket of the condenser, cooling the vapour so it condenses back to a liquid (the distillate).

questions.q: Fractional distillation is chosen over simple distillation when separating:
options: Two miscible liquids with close boiling points
questions.explain: The fractionating column lets liquids with similar (but different) boiling points separate; the one with the lower boiling point reaches the top and distils over first.

questions.q: In fractional distillation of a liquid mixture, which liquid is collected first?
options: The one with the lowest boiling point
The one with the highest boiling point
questions.explain: The liquid with the lowest boiling point evaporates most easily, passes up the column and is collected first.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, why must the baseline be drawn in pencil rather than pen?
options: Pen ink would dissolve and travel up the paper, ruining the result
questions.explain: Pencil (graphite) is insoluble and stays put, whereas pen ink would dissolve in the solvent and separate, interfering with the sample.

options: A solid phase and a gas phase
A stationary phase (the paper) and a mobile phase (the solvent)
A hot phase and a cold phase
An acid phase and a base phase
questions.explain: Separation depends on how substances distribute between the stationary phase (paper) and the mobile phase (solvent that moves through it).

questions.q: A spot travels 4.0 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. What is the Rf value?
questions.explain: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent = 4.0 / 8.0 = 0.5. Rf values are always between 0 and 1.

questions.q: On a chromatogram a substance produces a single spot in several different solvents. This suggests the substance is:
questions.explain: A pure substance gives one spot in any solvent. A mixture separates into more than one spot; testing in different solvents helps confirm purity.

questions.q: What does a higher Rf value tell you about a substance?
options: It is less soluble in the solvent
It is more soluble in the solvent and less attracted to the paper
questions.explain: A high Rf means the substance travels a long way with the solvent, so it is more soluble in the mobile phase and less strongly held by the paper.

questions.lo: melting point as a purity test
questions.q: A student measures a sample melting from 52 to 60 degrees C. The most likely conclusion is that the sample is:
options: Pure, with a sharp melting point
Impure or a mixture, because it melts over a range
questions.explain: Melting over a range (rather than at one sharp temperature) indicates impurity or a mixture. Impurities also usually lower the melting point.

questions.lo: melting point as a purity test
questions.q: Compared with the pure substance, an impurity usually causes the melting point to:
options: Decrease and spread over a range
questions.explain: Impurities lower the melting point and cause it to occur over a range of temperatures rather than sharply.

questions.q: A formulation is best described as:
options: A useful mixture with each component in a carefully measured quantity
An element in its standard state
A substance that cannot be separated
questions.explain: Formulations (e.g. paints, fuels, medicines, alloys) are mixtures made to a precise 'recipe' so each component contributes a specific property.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a formulation?
options: A single crystal of sodium chloride
A tablet of paracetamol containing binders, fillers and the active drug
questions.explain: A medicine tablet is a formulation: the active ingredient plus other components (fillers, binders) are combined in measured amounts to make a useful product.
